newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices rally as Iraq tension grows.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices rally as Iraq tension grows.

text.p: Crude oil prices ended higher on Tuesday as tensions built again about a U.S. military buildup in the Mideast Gulf, the largest oil producing area.
Concerns about cold weather in the Midwest helped bouy soybean prices, while corn closed lower. Pork belly and live hog futures closed higher on indications of tight supplies.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, October crude oil ended 12 cents a barrel higher at $23.31 after a senior Iraqi official said he expected a U.S. attack soon.
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz said the United States was beefing up its military presence in the Middle East Gulf to launch another military strike against Iraq country.
"American pretexts and excuses for the massing of troops and weapons in the Arab Gulf region are aimed at staging an aggression on Iraq," Aziz said.
Earlier, the United States sent a fresh warning to Iraq about interfering with Western maintenance of the no-fly zone over Iraq set up after the Gulf War in 1991.

Washington said two Patriot anti-missile batteries and U.S. soldiers to operate them had arrived in Saudi Arabia and President Clinton said he had ordered the deployment of extra troops to Kuwait on Monday night.
Oil prices rose sharply after Iraqi troops intervened in Kurdish factional fighting two weeks ago, prompting the United Nations to postpone allowing Iraqi oil sales to buy food.

A subsequent buildup of U.S. military might in the Gulf, which supplies 40 percent of world oil output, raised fears of supply disruptions and took October crude oil to a five-year high of $25.35 a barrel on Friday.

Prices tumbled on Monday, initially on perceptions of an easing of tension in the Gulf and later on an unfounded report that the United States had asked Saudi Arabia to raise production to compensate for the delay in Iraqi oil exports.
Gulf sources and the State Department denied any such request was made.
"The market is going to be choppy, but the fundamentals are in place," said Smith Barney's Saucer.
October heating oil closed up 0.30 cent to 65.59 cents a gallon but October gasoline ended down 0.13 cent to 62.74 cents a gallon.

At the Chicago Board of Trade fresh concerns about cold weather in the Midwest possibly hurting this year's late-planted soybean crop supported prices. November soybeans closed 3 cents a bushel higher at $7.96.

Traders said seesaw trading based on shifting weather forecasts was likely to continue this month as harvest gets under way from Ohio to Nebraska. The November contract had closed 9 cents per bushel lower on Monday.
"It was overdone yesterday. They acted as if the crop was harvested and in the bin, and the crop isn't even mature," said analyst Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.
A rumour that China was seeking 200,000 metric tons of U.S. soybeans for fall shipment also boosted sentiment.
Corn, which looks to be in better shape across the Midwest, closed mostly lower. September corn fell 5-3/4 cents a bushel at $3.51-1/4.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange pork belly and live hog futures closed higher on indications that supplies were becoming tighter. December live hogs closed 0.125 cent per pound higher at 55.675 cents and February pork bellies closed up 1.575 cents per pound at 76.55 cents.
"Bottom line, hog slaughter was heavy last week but it's not coming in heavy this week," said Dennis Smith, a livestock broker with trading company LIT America.
